title: 論語 季氏第十六
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 16, 〈季氏〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 16 of the Analects, 季氏 Jì shì, named, as every book is, from its first words — 'the Ji house', the great ministerial family of Lu that was about to attack the small dependency of Zhuanyu, while two of Confucius's disciples served in its household. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 16 has 14 passages and a manner of its own: the Master is called 孔子 'Kongzi' rather than 'the Master', and many sayings come in numbered sets — Zhu Xi quotes a Mr Hong (洪氏) for the view that some took this book to come from the lost Qi recension of the Analects. It opens with one of the longest exchanges in the Analects, Kongzi's rebuke of Ran You and Zilu over the planned attack: the holder of a state should fret not over having few people but over things being uneven, and the Ji's real trouble lies inside their own screen wall (16.1). Then come the decline of power from the Son of Heaven to the lords, the grandees and their retainers (16.2–3); three friends who do good and three who do harm, and three delights of each kind (16.4–5); the three things the gentleman holds in awe (16.8); the four grades of those who know (16.9); and the gentleman's nine thoughts (16.10). Near the end Kongzi's son Bo Yu tells how his father asked him in passing whether he had studied the Odes and the rites (16.13), and the book closes with the titles of a ruler's wife (16.14). Each numbered passage begins a new card; the long first passage is cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t: 季氏將伐顓臾。
sentences.l: The Ji house was about to attack Zhuanyu.
sentences.i: The Ji house was preparing to march on Zhuanyu.
sentences.n: The book is named 季氏 from its opening words. Zhu Xi's heading quotes Hong (洪氏): some take this book to come from the Qi version of the Analects, one of the texts current in Han times (此篇或以為齊論); fourteen chapters in all (凡十四章), and our numbers are his. Throughout the book the Master is called 孔子 'Kongzi', even with his own disciples, and several of its sayings are counted off in threes. 季氏 the Ji house is the Jisun, the strongest of the three great houses of Lu (3.1, 3.6, 11.16); its head at this time was presumably Ji Kangzi (12.17–19), whom Ran You served as steward, but the text names no one. 將 jiāng 'to be about to'; 伐 'to attack, make war on'. 顓臾 Zhuanyu is read zhuān yú (Zhu Xi: 顓音專臾音俞): a small state lying inside Lu, which Zhu Xi calls a dependency of Lu (顓臾國名魯附庸也) — a 附庸 was a minor state attached to a larger one, with no standing of its own at the royal court. He Yan's Kong Anguo: its rulers were descendants of Fu Xi with the surname Feng; it had been a dependency of Lu and was then subject to Lu; the Ji coveted its land and meant to destroy it and take it.

sentences.t:
冉有、季路見於孔子曰：「
季氏將有事於顓臾。」

morph.gloss: Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)
Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
clan, house (the family name as a lineage)

sentences.l:
Ran You and Ji Lu came before Kongzi and said:
“The Ji house is about to have business with Zhuanyu.”
sentences.i: Ran You and Ji Lu went to see Kongzi. “The Ji house,” they told him, “is going to move against Zhuanyu.”
sentences.n: 冉有 Ran You is Ran Qiu 冉求 (3.6), steward of the Ji house; 季路 Ji Lu is Zilu, Zhong You (5.25, 11.11). 見 is xiàn 'to present oneself, come before' (Zhu Xi: 見賢遍反), with 於 marking the man visited. 有事於 'to have business with' is a guarded way of saying the house means to use force: its servants do not say 'attack'. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Ran You and Ji Lu were servants of the Ji and came to tell Kongzi. Zhu Xi raises a difficulty: by the Zuo zhuan and the Records of the Historian the two did not serve the Ji at the same time (按左傳史記二子仕季氏不同時); that the text says so, he suspects (疑), is because Zilu once came back with Kongzi from Wei to Lu, served the Ji a second time, and before long went back to Wei.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
求！
無乃爾是過與？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said:
“Qiu!
Is it not rather you who are at fault?”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “Qiu, surely the blame for this lies with you?”
sentences.n: 求 Qiu is Ran You's personal name, used by his teacher. 無乃…與 'is it not rather…?' puts a reproach as a mild question, as 無乃…乎 does in 6.1 and 14.34; 與 is yú, the question particle (Zhu Xi: 與平聲). 爾是過: 爾 'you' stands before the verb 過 'to find fault with', and 是 takes it up — a way of putting an object first and stressing it: 'is it not you that (one must) fault?' Zhu Xi: Ran Qiu gathered in levies for the Ji (11.16) and was the one who above all ran their affairs, so the Master blamed him alone (冉求為季氏聚斂尤用事故夫子獨責之). He Yan's Kong Anguo is close: Ran Qiu was the Ji's steward, managing their house and gathering levies for them, so Kongzi suspected Qiu alone of having put them up to it (故孔子獨疑求教也).

sentences.t:
夫顓臾，
昔者先王以為東䝉主，
且在邦域之中矣；
是社稷之臣也；
何以伐為？

morph.gloss: (of) the altars of soil and grain
the altar of the soil, the shrine of the land god
millet, the god of the millet (社稷, 11.24)

sentences.i: Long ago the former kings set Zhuanyu to preside over the sacrifices of Mount Dongmeng. Besides, it lies inside our own borders, and it owes its service to the ducal house itself. Why make war on it?
sentences.n: The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment and are left unquoted. 夫 fú opens the topic, 'now, as for' (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶). 昔者 'in former days'. 以為 'took (it) to be, made it': 以 with its object understood, 為 wéi. 東䝉 Dongmeng (䝉 is the edition's form of 蒙 méng) is a mountain (Zhu Xi: 東䝉山名); the former kings enfeoffed Zhuanyu at its foot and set it to preside over its sacrifices, within the seven hundred li of Lu's land (先王封顓臾於此山之下使主其祭在魯地七百里之中). 主 is the master of a rite, the one who presides; Kong Anguo: they made it preside over the sacrifice to Mount Meng. 邦域之中 'within the bounds of the state'. 社稷 the altars of soil and grain (11.24) stand for the ruler's house: Zhu Xi, 社稷猶云公家, 'like saying the ducal house' — Zhuanyu served the Duke of Lu, not the Ji. 何以伐為 'what use is attacking it?' is the frame of 12.8 何以文為, with 為 wéi closing the question. Zhu Xi sets out the background: Lu had been divided in four, the Ji taking two parts and the Mengsun and Shusun one each (是時四分魯國季氏取其二孟孫叔孫各有其一); only the dependency still served the duke, and the Ji wanted it to enlarge themselves. So the three clauses are three reasons: a state enfeoffed by the former kings may not be attacked; one within the bounds need not be; a servant of the altars is not the Ji's to attack (顓臾乃先王封國則不可伐在邦域之中則不必伐是社稷之臣則非季氏所當伐也). Here, he says, the right of the matter is fixed beyond change, and a word gives its every turn, as none but a sage could. Variant: He Yan's text reads 何以為伐也, 'why do the attacking?'; Kong Anguo: it already belongs to Lu as a servant of the altars — what use destroying it (何用滅之為也)?

sentences.t:
冉有曰：「
夫子欲之，
吾二臣者皆不欲也。」

morph.gloss: Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)

sentences.i: Ran You said: “It is our lord who wants it. Neither of us two who serve him does.”
sentences.n: 夫子 fū zǐ, the disciples' word for the Master, here means the man they serve: Zhu Xi, 夫子指季孫, 'points to Jisun', as at 14.38. 吾二臣者 'we two servants': 臣 is a household retainer (14.19), and 者 sets the phrase off as the topic; 皆 'both, all'. Zhu Xi: Ran You had in fact taken part in the plan (冉有實與謀), and because the Master condemned it he laid the blame on the Ji. Kong Anguo says only that he put the blame on the Ji.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
求！
周任有言曰：『
陳力就列，
不能者止。』
危而不持，
顛而不扶，
則將焉用彼相矣？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said:
“Qiu!
Zhou Ren had a saying:
‘Lay out your strength and go to your place;
one who cannot, stops.’
Tottering, and not held up;
falling, and not steadied —
then what use will one make of that helper?”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “Qiu, Zhou Ren used to say: ‘Put all your strength into it and then take your post; if you cannot, leave off.’ If the blind man stumbles and no one holds him, if he falls and no one catches him, what is the man leading him for?”
sentences.n: The quotation inside the Master's words is marked ‘ ’. 周任 Zhou Ren (任 rén; Zhu Xi: 任平聲) was, Zhu Xi says, a good archivist of old (古之良史); He Yan's Ma Rong calls him a good officer of old (古之良吏). 陳 chén 'to lay out, spread' (Zhu Xi: 陳布也) and 列 liè 'a place in the ranks, a post' (列位也): put out the whole of one's strength, and so take one's place; 不能者止 'one who cannot, stops'. It is the 止 of 11.23 (不可則止), where the Master says a great minister stops when the Way cannot be followed, and finds Yóu and Qiu ministers who only fill out the number. Ma Rong: one should set forth one's abilities, weigh what one can take on, and so go to one's post; if one cannot, one should stop. 相 is xiàng (Zhu Xi: 相去聲, and 'the same below', 下同), here the helper who leads a blind man (相瞽者之相也), as at 15.41: 危 'to totter', 持 chí 'to hold up', 顛 'to fall headlong', 扶 fú 'to prop, steady'. 將 jiāng 'will, is going to'; 焉 yān 'how, to what end' (Zhu Xi: 於虔反); 彼相 'that helper'. Zhu Xi: if the two did not want it, they should have remonstrated, and if remonstrance was not heeded, they should have left. Bao Xian in He Yan: one who helps a man should hold him when he totters and steady him when he falls; if he cannot, what use is his helping?

sentences.t:
且爾言過矣。
虎兕出於柙，
龜玉毁於櫝中，
是誰之過與？
sentences.l:
And besides, your words are wrong.
A tiger or wild ox gets out of its cage,
tortoise shell or jade is broken inside its casket —
whose fault is this?
sentences.i: And what you say is wrong besides. When a tiger or a wild ox breaks out of its pen, or turtle shell and jade are smashed in the chest that holds them, who is to answer for it?
sentences.n: The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment and are left unquoted. 過 here is 'wrong, mistaken'; in the last clause it is 'fault'. 兕 sì (Zhu Xi: 徐履反) is a wild ox (兕野牛也); 柙 xiá (户甲反) a cage or pen for beasts (柙檻也; Ma Rong the same). 龜 guī is tortoise shell, used in divination, and 玉 jade, the tokens of rank: the treasures of a house. 櫝 dú (音獨) is a casket (櫝匱也). 毁 'to be broken' — the same graph as 'to run down' in 15.24. 是誰之過與 'this is whose fault?', with 與 yú the question particle (Zhu Xi: 與平聲). Zhu Xi: if a thing in the cage gets loose or a thing in the casket is broken, those whose charge it was to keep it cannot escape the fault; this makes plain that if the two hold their posts and do not leave, they cannot help bearing the blame for the Ji's wrong (明二子居其位而不去則季氏之惡己不得不任其責也). Ma Rong: is it not the keepers' fault? He Yan's text reads 龜玉毀櫝中, without 於; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
冉有曰：「
今夫顓臾，
固而近於費。
今不取，
後世必為子孫憂。」

morph.gloss: Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)

sentences.l:
Ran You said:
“Now, Zhuanyu —
it is strong-walled and near Bi.
If it is not taken now,
in later generations it will surely be a worry to sons and grandsons.”
sentences.i: Ran You said: “But Zhuanyu is well fortified, and close to Bi. Leave it untaken now, and it is bound to trouble the house's heirs in time to come.”
sentences.n: 今夫 'now, as for…': 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶) points to the topic. 固 'firm': Zhu Xi, its walls are whole and strong (固謂城郭完固); Ma Rong adds sharp weapons and sound armour. 費 Bi, read bì (Zhu Xi at 6.7: 費音秘), was the Ji's own walled town (Zhu Xi: 費季氏之私邑; 6.7, 11.24). 為 wéi 'to become'; 子孫 'sons and grandsons', the house's descendants; 憂 'a worry'. Zhu Xi: this is Ran Qiu's dressed-up excuse (此則冉求之餙辭 — 餙 is the print's form of 飾), yet it also shows that he really did share in the Ji's plan (然亦可見其實與季氏之謀矣).

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
求！
君子疾夫舍曰『欲之』而必為之辭。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said:
“Qiu!
The gentleman hates that — setting aside saying ‘We want it’, and insisting on making up words for it.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “Qiu, what a gentleman cannot bear is the man who will not say outright ‘I want it’ but must have a story to cover it.”
sentences.n: 疾 'to hate' (as 14.34). 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶) is 'that', pointing ahead to what follows. 舍 shě 'to set aside, leave out' (Zhu Xi: 舍上聲); 曰欲之 'saying “(we) want it”' — Zhu Xi: wanting it means coveting its profit (欲之謂貪其利). 必 'must, insists on'; 為之辭 'to make words for it', 為 wéi, 辭 'words, a speech': an excuse. Kong Anguo: 疾如汝之言也, he hates speech like yours — to set aside the talk of coveting gain and make up other words instead is what he hates. He Yan's text reads 必更爲之辞 'must make up other words for it', the reading Kong Anguo explains (更作佗辭).

sentences.t:
丘也聞有國有家者，
不患寡而患不均，
不患貧而患不安。
盖均無貧，
和無寡，
安無傾。
sentences.i: I have heard that whoever holds a state or a noble house is not troubled that his people are few, but that each does not have his due share; not troubled that wealth is scarce, but that high and low are not at rest with one another. For where shares are even, no one is poor; where people are at ease together, they are not too few; and where all are settled, nothing topples.
sentences.n: The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment and are left unquoted. (The ○ before 丘也聞 in the print is not one of Zhu Xi's chapter marks: his count of fourteen needs this chapter to run on to 蕭牆之内也.) 丘也 'I, Qiu': the Master uses his own name, 也 a pause. 有國有家者 'those who have a state, have a house': Kong Anguo, 國 are the feudal lords, 家 the ministers and grandees. 患 'to be troubled by, fret over'. Zhu Xi's glosses: 寡 is few people (寡謂民少), 貧 short of wealth (貧謂財乏), 均 jūn each getting his share (均謂各得其分), 安 high and low at ease with one another (安謂上下相安). 盖 gài (the edition's form of 蓋) 'for, it is that' gives the reason. 和 is ease among people, as in 13.23; 傾 qīng 'to lean over, topple'. Zhu Xi: the Ji wanted Zhuanyu only because they fretted over too few people and too little wealth; but at this time the Ji held the state and the Duke of Lu had no people — that is not even (季氏據國而魯公無民則不均矣); the lord weak, the minister strong, each breeding suspicion of the other — that is not settled. Even, one does not fret over poverty, and there is ease; at ease, one does not fret over fewness, and all are settled; settled, high and low do not suspect each other, and there is no danger of overturning. Bao Xian in He Yan reads the last line the same way: government even, high and low at one, great and small at peace, and none of the three ills follows. Variant: He Yan's text reads 均無貪, 'even, there is no greed', and Bao Xian's comment there has 不患貪 to match; since 貧 stands just above, the copy has probably slipped to the near-identical 貪, though that is a guess.

sentences.t:
夫如是，
故逺人不服，
則脩文徳以來之；
既來之，
則安之。
sentences.l:
Now, it being so,
therefore, if far-off people do not submit,
then cultivate the virtue of letters to bring them;
once they are brought,
then settle them.
sentences.i: That is how it stands. So when people at a distance will not come over, rely on the virtue of peace and learning to draw them in; and once they have come, give them a settled life.
sentences.n: The Master's words run on. 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶) 'now'; 如是 'being like this', the state just described. 逺人 'people far off' (逺 is the edition's form of 遠, here plain yuǎn), the 逺者 of 13.16. 服 'to submit, be won over'. 脩 'to put in order, cultivate' (= 修). 文徳 is virtue of the civil kind, letters as against arms; Zhu Xi's comment says simply 脩徳. 來之 'make them come' and 安之 'settle them, give them peace' are both causative, with 之 'them' as object. 既 'once, when already'. Zhu Xi: only when order within is put right do people far off submit; if some do not, one cultivates virtue to bring them, and should not wear out troops far afield either (内治脩然後逺人服有不服則脩徳以來之亦不當勤兵於逺).

sentences.t:
今由與求也，
相夫子，
逺人不服而不能來也；
邦分崩離析而不能守也；
sentences.i: Now you two, Yóu and Qiu, are your master's helpers. People at a distance will not come over, and you cannot draw them in; the state is breaking up piece by piece, and you cannot keep it whole;
sentences.n: The Master's words run on. 由 Yóu is Zilu's personal name and 求 Qiu Ran You's, as in 11.23 今由與求也 'Now Yóu and Qiu', which opens a like complaint; 與 yǔ 'and'. 相 xiàng 'to assist' (Zhu Xi's 相去聲, 下同 covers it); 夫子 is again the head of the Ji, the master they serve. Zhu Xi: though Zilu took no part in the plan, he had never been able to steer the Ji by what is right, so he too cannot be held blameless, and the Master blames both together (子路雖不與謀而素不能輔之以義亦不得為無罪故并責之). He takes the 'people far off' to be Zhuanyu (逺人謂顓臾). 分崩離析 is four verbs of breaking apart: 分 fēn 'to divide', 崩 bēng 'to crumble, collapse', 離 lí 'to part', 析 xī 'to split'. Zhu Xi: the ducal house divided in four, and the house retainers in revolt time and again (謂四分公室家臣屢叛). Kong Anguo takes them of the people: divided in heart, wanting to leave, no longer to be gathered together. 守 'to hold, keep'.

sentences.t:
而謀動干戈於邦内。
吾恐季孫之憂，
不在顓臾，
而在蕭牆之内也。
sentences.l:
and yet you plan to set shields and dagger-axes moving within the state.
I fear that Jisun's worry
lies not in Zhuanyu
but inside the screen wall.
sentences.i: and yet you are plotting to take up arms inside the country's own borders. My fear is that the Jisun's troubles will come not from Zhuanyu but from inside his own court, on the near side of the screen wall.
sentences.n: The Master's words run on to the end of the chapter. 而 'and yet'. 謀 'to plan'; 動干戈 'to set shield and dagger-axe in motion', to take up arms: Zhu Xi, 干 is a shield (干楯也) and 戈 gē a dagger-axe (戈㦸也 — 㦸 the print's form of 戟); Kong Anguo the same. 邦内 'inside the state': Zhuanyu lies within Lu. 季孫 Jisun is the head of the Ji (14.38). 蕭牆 xiāo qiáng is the screen wall standing inside a gate (Zhu Xi: 蕭牆屏也). Zheng Xuan in He Yan: 蕭之言肅也, 蕭 means 'solemn' — at audience, ruler and minister reached the screen and took on a more reverent bearing, hence the name; so 'inside the screen wall' points to the court of Lu itself. Zhu Xi: with no evenness and no ease (不均不和), trouble from within was about to break out; and afterwards Duke Ai did in fact want to use Yue to attack Lu and be rid of the Ji (其後哀公果欲以越伐魯而去季氏). Zheng Xuan's instance is the Ji's retainer Yang Hu imprisoning Ji Huanzi. Zhu Xi ends with two voices. Xie Liangzuo: the Three Families (3.2) were strong and the ducal house weak, and Ran Qiu meant to attack Zhuanyu to add to them still more; the Master condemned him so deeply because he was starving Lu to fatten the Three Families (為其瘠魯以肥三家也). Hong: the two served the Ji and must have told the Master whatever the Ji meant to do, so many things were likely saved or stopped by his words; the attack on Zhuanyu is not found in the classics or their commentaries — perhaps it was stopped by what the Master said here (其以夫子之言而止也與). He Yan's text reads 不在於顓臾, adding 於; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
天下有道則
禮樂征伐自天子出；
天下無道則
禮樂征伐自諸侯出。
自諸侯出，盖十世希不失矣；
自大夫出，五世希不失矣；
陪臣執國命，三世希不失矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the fused 之於 'it to, it at'
a lord, a feudal prince, ruler of a state (諸侯, 11.25)
the fused 之於 'it to, it at'
a lord, a feudal prince, ruler of a state (諸侯, 11.25)

sentences.i: Kongzi said: “When the world is on the Way, the rites and music, and the making of war on those who do wrong, are ordered by the Son of Heaven. When the world has left the Way, they are ordered by the feudal lords. Once they are in the lords' hands, it will be a rare house that keeps hold of them for as long as ten generations; once they are in the grandees' hands, a rare house that keeps them five; and when the grandees' own retainers take charge of the state's commands, a rare one that keeps them three.”
sentences.n: 孔子曰 'Kongzi said', as in every saying of the Master in this book (see 16.1). 天下有道 / 無道 'the world has / lacks the Way' (as 8.13). 禮樂 'the rites and music', 樂 yuè (as 11.1, 13.3). 征 zhēng is to march against, to bring force to bear on those who have done wrong, and 伐 'to attack'; together, the right of making war. 自…出 'issue from'. 盖 gài is the edition's form of 蓋 'likely, roughly'. 十世希不失矣 'in ten generations, rarely do they not lose (it)': 希 'rare' (Kong Anguo in He Yan: 希少也), 不失 'not lose'. 世 here is a generation of rulers in one house (not Zhu Xi's 'dynasty' of 2.23). 陪臣 péi chén are the retainers of the grandees, a vassal's vassal: Zhu Xi: 陪臣家臣也; Ma Rong in He Yan: 陪 is 'doubled' (陪重也). 國命 'the state's commands'. Zhu Xi: by the institutions of the former kings, the lords could not alter the rites and music nor take campaigns into their own hands (先王之制諸侯不得變禮樂專征伐); the further one goes against principle, the faster it is lost (逆理愈甚則其失之愈速), and the numbers of generations are roughly no more than these (大約世數不過如此). He Yan's commentators count them out in history: Kong Anguo, that after King You was killed and King Ping moved east the Zhou grew weak and the lords made their own rites and music, and in Lu from Duke Yin to Duke Zhao ten generations passed before Duke Zhao lost his government and died in exile at Ganhou; and that from Ji Wenzi, who first took the government, to Ji Huanzi was five generations, when Huanzi was made prisoner by his own retainer Yang Hu; Ma Rong, that the Yang were retainers of the Ji for three generations until Hu fled to Qi. Kongzi's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next two units are left unquoted.

sentences.t:
天下有道則
政不在大夫。
sentences.l:
When the world has the Way, then
government does not lie with the grandees.
sentences.i: When the world is on the Way, government is not in the hands of the grandees.
sentences.n: Still Kongzi, unquoted. 政 'government'; 不在大夫 'is not with the grandees'. Zhu Xi: that is, they may not take the government into their own hands (言不得專政). Kong Anguo in He Yan: its control comes from the ruler (制之由君也).

sentences.t:
天下有道則
庶人不議。
sentences.l:
When the world has the Way, then
the common people do not find fault.
sentences.i: When the world is on the Way, the common people have no complaints to make about their government.
sentences.n: Still Kongzi, unquoted. 庶人 shù rén 'the common people', the many who hold no rank. 議 'to debate, to criticize'. Zhu Xi: when those above make no failures in government, those below have no private criticism — it is not that their mouths are clamped so that they dare not speak (上無失政則下無私議非箝其口使不敢言也); and of the whole chapter: it treats in general the course of the world (此章通論天下之勢). Kong Anguo in He Yan: they have nothing to find fault with (無所非議也).

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
禄之去公室，五世矣；
政逮於大夫四世矣；
故夫三桓之子孫，微矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
(makes 'salary leaving the ducal house' one phrase)

sentences.i: Kongzi said: “For five generations the giving of rank and pay has been out of the ducal house's hands, and for four generations government has rested with the grandees. That is why the descendants of the three Huan houses are themselves now in decline.”
sentences.n: 禄 'salary', here the ruler's power to grant rank and pay: Zheng Xuan in He Yan says rank and salary no longer came from the ruler (爵禄不從君出). 之 makes 禄之去公室 'salary's leaving the ducal house' one phrase; 去 qù 'to go from'; 公室 'the ducal house'. 逮 dài 'to reach' (Zhu Xi: 逮及也). 夫 fú 'those', pointing (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶). 三桓 sān huán, the Three Huan, are the three great houses of Lu, the Three Families of 3.2: Kong Anguo in He Yan: Zhongsun, Shusun and Jisun, all three ministers descended from Duke Huan, hence the name (三卿皆出桓公也故曰三桓也); the Zhongsun later took the name Meng. 微 'small', so 'to dwindle'. Zhu Xi counts the generations: from the death of Duke Wen, when Prince Sui killed (the heir) Chi and set up Duke Xuan, the ruler of Lu lost his government, through Cheng, Xiang, Zhao and Ding, five dukes in all; from Ji Wuzi the Ji began to hold the government of the state, through Daozi, Pingzi and Huanzi, four generations in all, and then (Huanzi) was seized by his retainer Yang Hu. This, he says, was worked out from the previous chapter's account (此以前章之説推之而知其當然也); this chapter speaks of Lu alone, and he suspects both were said in Duke Ding's time (疑與前章皆定公時語). He quotes Su Shi: when the lords take over the rites and the campaigns they should grow strong, yet Lu lost its government; when government comes down to the grandees they should grow strong, yet the Three Huan dwindled — why? Strength comes from security, and security from a settled division between above and below (强生於安安生於上下之分定); now lords and grandees alike overrode those above them, so had nothing to command those below with, and none lasted. Zheng Xuan counts differently: the five generations from Xiangzhong's killing of Chi to Duke Ding, and the four as Wenzi, Wuzi, Daozi and Pingzi (文子武子悼子平子也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 政逮大夫, without 於.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
益者三友，
損者三友。
友直，友諒，友多聞，益矣；
友便辟，友善柔，友便佞，損矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said:
“Bringing gain, three friends;
bringing loss, three friends.
Take as friend the straight, take as friend the sincere, take as friend one who has heard much: gain.
Take as friend the practised but crooked, take as friend the skilled in softness, take as friend the practised smooth talker: loss.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “Of friends, three will do you good and three will do you harm. A friend who is straight with you, a friend who means what he says, a friend who has heard a great deal: these do you good. A friend all polished manners and no straightness, a friend all soft compliance, a friend all glib talk: these do you harm.”
sentences.n: 益者三友 'the ones bringing gain are three friends': 者 turns 益 'to add, to profit' into 'what brings gain', and 損 'to take away' is its opposite. 友 is then the verb 'to befriend, take as friend' (as 1.8 無友不如己者), each time with its object: 直 'the straight'; 諒 liàng, here in its good sense, 'the sincere, the one true to his word' — not the 'petty good faith' of 14.18 and 15.36; 多聞 'one who has heard much'. 益矣 / 損矣 'is gain / is loss'. 便 is pián (Zhu Xi: 便平聲); for 辟 he gives 婢亦反, a voiced initial; modern practice reads it pì. Zhu Xi: befriend the straight and you hear of your faults; befriend the sincere and you advance toward integrity; befriend the much-heard and you advance toward clear understanding (友直則聞其過友諒則進於誠友多聞則進於明). 便 is 'practised, at home in' (便習熟也): 便辟 is being practised in deportment but not straight (習於威儀而不直); 善柔 is being skilled at fawning and pleasing but not sincere (工於媚説而不諒); 便佞 is being practised in talk but without the substance of things heard and seen (習於口語而無聞見之實). The three that harm are the exact opposites of the three that help. He quotes Yin Tun: from the Son of Heaven down to the common people, no one has ever been made without friends, and their gain and loss is like this — can one fail to take care? He Yan's text writes 便僻, and Ma Rong reads it as skilfully dodging what others dislike in order to win favour (便巧辟人所忌以求容媚也), 辟 as 'to avoid'; Ma Rong takes 善柔 as 'soft in the face' (面柔也), and Zheng Xuan 便佞 as glib and fluent (便辨也謂佞而辨也).

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
益者三樂，
損者三樂。
樂節禮樂，樂道人之善，樂多賢友，益矣；
樂驕樂，樂佚遊，樂宴樂，損矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said:
“Bringing gain, three delights;
bringing loss, three delights.
Delighting in measuring out the rites and music, delighting in speaking of others' good, delighting in many worthy friends: gain.
Delighting in proud pleasure, delighting in idle roaming, delighting in feasting pleasure: loss.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “There are three kinds of liking that do a man good and three that do him harm. To like keeping the rites and music to their true measure, to like talking about the good in others, to like having many friends of worth: these do good. To like the pleasures of pride, to like drifting about at leisure, to like the pleasures of the banquet: these do harm.”
sentences.n: Built like 16.4, with 樂 in place of 友. Zhu Xi's sound notes decide each 樂: it is yào 'to delight in' (樂五教反), both as the verb and as the 'delights' that are counted; in 禮樂 it is yuè 'music' (禮樂之樂音岳); in 驕樂 and 宴樂 it is lè 'pleasure' (驕樂宴樂之樂音洛). Modern practice keeps all three. 節 is a verb, 'to give due measure to': Zhu Xi: 節 means distinguishing the measures of their institutions, sounds and bearing (節謂辨其制度聲容之節); He Yan's own comment: in every movement to attain the measure of the rites and music (動得禮樂之節也). 道 dào 'to speak of' (as 14.30 自道); 人之善 'others' good points'. 驕 'proud'; 佚 yì 'idle, dissolute'; 遊 'to roam'; 宴 yàn 'to feast'. Zhu Xi: with proud pleasure one grows extravagant and unbridled and knows no measure (侈肆而不知節); with idle roaming, lazy and slack and hating to hear of good (惰慢而惡聞善); with feasting pleasure, sunk in excess and familiar with small men (淫溺而狎小人) — the three are again the opposites of the three that help. He quotes Yin Tun: in what the gentleman likes and delights in, can he fail to take care (君子之於好樂可不謹哉)? Wang Su in He Yan: idle roaming is going out and coming in without measure (佚遊出入不知節也); Kong Anguo: feasting pleasure is sinking into dissipation, and the three are the way to harm oneself (三者自損之道也).

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
侍於君子有三愆：
言未及之而言，謂之躁；
言及之而不言，謂之隠；
未見顔色而言，謂之瞽。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Kongzi said: “When you wait upon a gentleman there are three mistakes to be made. To speak up before the talk has reached you is called being hasty. To keep quiet when it has reached you is called being close. To speak before you have read his face is called talking like a blind man.”
sentences.n: 侍 'to attend on (a superior)'. Here 君子 is not only a man of character: Zhu Xi: 君子 is the general name for one who has virtue and rank (君子有徳位之通稱). 愆 qiān 'a fault, an error' (Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo in He Yan: 愆過也). The three cases are built alike: a situation, 而 'and yet', 言 'speaking' or 不言 'not speaking', then 謂之X 'one calls it X'. 言未及之 'the talk has not yet come to it (to you)'. 躁 zào 'hasty, restless' (Zheng Xuan in He Yan: 躁不安静也). 隠 is the edition's form of 隱 'to hide' (Kong Anguo: 隱匿不盡情實也, hiding and not giving the whole truth). 顔色 'the look on the face' (as 10.4); 瞽 gǔ 'blind'. Zhu Xi: the blind have no eyes and cannot weigh words or watch the face (瞽無目不能察言觀色; cf. 12.20 察言而觀色). He quotes Yin Tun: speak only when it is time, and there will be none of the three errors (時然後言則無三者之過矣) — the words said of Gongshu Wenzi at 14.14. Zhou Shenglie in He Yan: speaking before seeing which way the gentleman's look inclines, and running ahead of his thoughts, is like being blind. Variant: He Yan's text reads 言及之不言, without 而.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
君子有三戒：
少之時，血氣未定，戒之在色；
及其壯也，血氣方剛，戒之在鬭；
及其老也，血氣既衰，戒之在得。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Kongzi said: “The gentleman keeps watch on himself at three points. While he is young and his blood and breath have not yet settled, he watches himself with women. In his prime, when blood and breath run at their hottest, he watches himself in quarrels. When he is old and blood and breath are running down, he watches himself with gain.”
sentences.n: 戒 jiè 'to be on guard against, to take warning'. 少 shào 'young'; 少之時 'the time of being young'. 血氣 xuè qì 'blood and breath': Zhu Xi: what the bodily frame depends on to live, blood being yin and breath yang (血氣形之所待以生者血隂而氣陽也). 戒之在色 'guarding against it lies in women': 之 is the object of 戒, and 在 says where the danger lies. 色 'beauty, women' (as 9.17). 壯 zhuàng 'the full strength of manhood'; 方 'just then'; 剛 'hard, unyielding'; 鬭 dòu is the edition's form of 鬥 'to fight, to brawl'; 既衰 'already declining' (衰 shuāi). 得 'getting': Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo in He Yan both say 得 is greed for gain (得貪得也). Zhu Xi: know the warning proper to each season of life and master it by principle, and one is not driven by blood and breath (隨時知戒以理勝之則不為血氣所使也). He quotes Fan Zuyu: the sage is the same as other men in blood and breath and different in the breath of his will (志氣); blood and breath have their time of failing, the breath of the will never fails; the gentleman nourishes the breath of his will and so is not moved by blood and breath, and so the higher his years, the loftier his virtue (年彌髙而徳彌邵也).

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
君子有三畏：
畏天命，
畏大人，
畏聖人之言。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said:
“The gentleman has three things he holds in awe:
he holds in awe the decree of Heaven,
holds in awe great men,
holds in awe the words of the sages.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “Three things put the gentleman in awe: what Heaven has ordained, great men, and the sayings of the sages.”
sentences.n: 畏 'to hold in awe': Zhu Xi: 畏 has the sense of grave dread (畏者嚴憚之意也). 天命 'the decree of Heaven' (as 2.4): Zhu Xi here: the right principle that Heaven endows (天所賦之正理也); know that it is to be feared and one's caution and dread will of themselves not cease, and the weight of what one has been entrusted with need not be lost (付畀之重可以不失矣). 大人 dà rén 'great men'; 聖人之言 'the words of the sages'. Zhu Xi does not define 大人, but says that great men and the sages' words are both things the decree of Heaven makes one fear, so that whoever knows to fear the decree of Heaven cannot help fearing them (大人聖言皆天命所當畏知畏天命則不得不畏之矣). He Yan's own comments: follow it and fortune comes, defy it and disaster — that is Heaven's decree (順吉逆凶天之命也); great men are the sages, one with Heaven and Earth in virtue (大人即聖人與天地合其德者也); the sages' words are deep and far and not easily known (深逺不可易知則聖人之言也). Kongzi's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
小人不知天命而不畏也，
狎大人，
侮聖人之言。
sentences.i: The small man does not know what Heaven has ordained, and so has no awe of it; he is free and easy with great men, and makes light of what the sages said.
sentences.n: Still Kongzi, unquoted: the small man reverses each of the gentleman's three. 狎 xiá 'to be on easy terms, to take liberties' (as 10.16); 侮 wǔ: Zhu Xi: 侮戲玩也 'to toy with, to make game of'. Zhu Xi: not knowing the decree of Heaven, he does not recognize what principle requires, and has nothing he dreads (不識義理而無所忌憚如此). He quotes Yin Tun: the three awes are what sincerity in cultivating oneself makes natural; the small man does not work at cultivating himself, so what awe could he have (小人不務脩身誠已則何畏之有)? He Yan's own comments: being careless and slack, he does not know to fear (恢䟽故不知畏也); great men are straightforward and not overbearing, so he takes liberties with them (直而不肆故狎之也); the sages' words cannot be known in a small way, so he makes game of them (不可小知故侮之也).

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
生而知之者，上也；
學而知之者，次也；
困而學之，又其次也；
困而不學，民斯為下矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Kongzi said: “Those who know it without being taught stand highest. Those who come to know it by study stand next. Those who take to study only when they find themselves stuck come after them. And those who are stuck and still will not study — that is where the common run of people stand, at the bottom.”
sentences.n: 生而知之者 'those who know it from birth', the phrase the Master refuses for himself at 7.19, with the same English. 上 'the highest'; 次 'the next' (as 13.20 其次); 又其次 'again the next after that'. 困 kùn: Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo in He Yan: 困 is having something one cannot get through (困謂有所不通). 民斯為下矣 'the common folk thereby count as the lowest': 斯 'thereby, then'; 為 wéi 'to count as'. The line is usually taken to say that those who are stuck and will not learn are the ordinary run of people, and rank lowest. Zhu Xi: men's endowments differ, and roughly come in these four grades (言人之氣質不同大約有此四等). He quotes Yang Shi: from knowing at birth and knowing by learning down to learning when stuck, the endowments are not the same, but once they know it, it is one (及其知之一也); so the gentleman values learning above all, and only being stuck and not learning makes one the lowest (困而不學然後為下).

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「
君子有九思：
視思明，聽思聰，
色思溫，貌思恭，
言思忠，事思敬，
疑思問，忿思難，
見得思義。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Kongzi said: “Nine things are always in the gentleman's mind. When he looks, that he see clearly; when he listens, that he hear sharply; that his face be mild and his bearing respectful; that his words be wholehearted and his work done with reverent care. In doubt, he thinks to ask; in anger, he thinks of the trouble it may bring; and when there is gain in sight, he thinks of what is right.”
sentences.n: Nine clauses of one shape, X思Y 'in X, he thinks of Y'. 明 'clear (of sight)'; 聰 cōng 'keen (of hearing)'. Zhu Xi: when sight is blocked by nothing, its clearness sees everything; when hearing is stopped by nothing, its keenness hears everything (視無所蔽則明無不見聽無所壅則聰無不聞); 色 is what shows in the face, 貌 is said of the whole body (色見於面者貌舉身而言). 溫 'mild', 恭 'respectful', 忠 'wholehearted', 敬 'reverent care'. 難 is nàn, 'trouble, what comes after' (Zhu Xi: 難去聲): think of asking, and doubt is not stored up; think of the trouble, and anger is sure to be checked (cf. 12.21 一朝之忿); think of what is right, and getting is not careless (思問則疑不蓄思難則忿必懲思義則得不苟). 見得思義 is 14.13's 見利思義 'seeing gain, he thinks of what is right' with 得 'something to get' for 利. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: each of the nine thoughts attends to its one thing (九思各專其一); and Xie Liangzuo: until one reaches ease, hitting the Way without effort, there is no moment when one does not examine oneself; even so, the times it is not present are few (雖有不存焉者寡矣) — this is what is called 'thinking to be sincere' (此之謂思誠). He Yan has no comment on the chapter.

sentences.t:
孔子曰：「『
見善如不及，
見不善如探湯。』
吾見其人矣，
吾聞其語矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi said:
“‘Seeing the good as though not catching up with it,
seeing the not-good as though feeling into boiling water’ —
I have seen men like that;
I have heard the words.”
sentences.i: Kongzi said: “‘He sees what is good and goes after it as though he might never catch it; he sees what is not good and shies away as from scalding water.’ I have seen men like that, and I have heard the saying.”
sentences.n: 如不及 'as though not reaching (it)', as in 8.17 學如不及. 探 tàn 'to feel into, to test with the hand' (Zhu Xi: 吐南反, a level tone, tān; modern tàn); 湯 'boiling water'. Zhu Xi: truly to know good and bad and sincerely love the one and hate the other — the likes of Yan Hui, Master Zeng, Min Ziqian and Ran probably managed it (顔曽閔冉之徒葢能之矣); and 語 is probably an old saying (語葢古語也), so the two lines are set off as a quotation. 其人 'such men', 其語 'the words'. Kong Anguo in He Yan: 探湯 stands for getting away from evil (the rest of his comment is garbled in the transcription). Kongzi's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted. Variant: He Yan's text reads 吾聞其語, without the first 矣.

sentences.t:
隠居以求其志，
行義以達其道：
吾聞其語矣，
未見其人也。
sentences.l:
Living hidden to seek out his aim,
doing what is right to carry his Way through:
I have heard the words,
but have not seen such a man.
sentences.i: He lives out of sight to hold to what his heart is set on, and does what is right to carry his Way through to the end: that saying I have heard, but such a man I have yet to see.
sentences.n: Still Kongzi, unquoted; a second saying, set against the first: of that one he has seen the men, of this one only heard the words. 隠居 'to dwell hidden' (隠 is the edition's form of 隱); 以 'so as to'; 求其志 'seek out his aim'; 行 xíng 'to do'; 達其道 'carry his Way through' (達 'to get through'). Zhu Xi: seeking his aim is keeping the Way he would carry through; carrying his Way through is putting into practice the aim he sought (求其志守其所達之道也達其道行其所求之志也); probably only men of the stamp of Yi Yin and the Taigong could fit it (葢惟伊尹太公之流可以當之); in that day Yan Hui came close, but he stayed hidden and was not seen, and had the misfortune to die young, so the Master spoke as he did. Yi Yin was minister to Tang (12.22); the Taigong, in tradition, was the adviser of King Wen and King Wu of Zhou. 未見其人也 'have not seen such a man', against the first unit's 吾見其人矣.

sentences.t:
齊景公有馬千駟，
死之日，民無徳而稱焉。
伯夷、叔齊餓于首陽之下，
民到于今稱之。

morph.gloss: to make even, to bring to one standard (Zhu Xi: 所以一之也)
the Yi, the peoples of the east
to make even, to bring to one standard (Zhu Xi: 所以一之也)

sentences.i: Duke Jing of Qi owned four thousand horses, yet when he died the people could find no virtue in him to praise. Boyi and Shuqi starved to death below Mount Shouyang, and the people praise them to this day.
sentences.n: No speaker is named; Zhu Xi thinks 孔子曰 has dropped out (see the next unit). 齊景公 Duke Jing of Qi is the ruler of 12.11. 駟 sì 'a team of four' (Zhu Xi: 駟四馬也), so a thousand teams is four thousand horses (Kong Anguo in He Yan: 千駟四千匹也). 死之日 'the day of his death'. 民無徳而稱焉 'the people had no virtue to praise him by': 焉 'him, in him'. 伯夷 Boyi and 叔齊 Shuqi (5.22, 7.14) are the brothers who, by the story Zhu Xi tells at 7.14, starved on Mount Shouyang rather than eat the grain of Zhou. 餓 è 'to starve'; 首陽 shǒu yáng, a mountain (Zhu Xi: 首陽山名; Ma Rong in He Yan places it in Hedong, north of Mount Hua, in the bend of the Yellow River). 于 = 於; 到于今 'down to now' (as 14.18). 稱 chēng 'to praise'. Variant: Ruan's text and He Yan's read 民無得而稱焉 'the people found nothing to praise him for' — the very words said of Taibo at 8.1, where his virtue was too great to name; here it would be the opposite, nothing to name at all.

sentences.t: 其斯之謂與？
sentences.l: Is it this that is meant?
sentences.i: Is this not what is meant?
sentences.n: The same words as Zigong's at 1.15, and the same l: 斯 'this' is the object of 謂 'to mean', fronted and marked by 之; 其 at the head softens it to a guess, and 與 is the question particle yú (Zhu Xi: 與平聲). But what is 'this'? Nothing in the chapter is a saying to point back to. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: Master Cheng held that the couplet 誠不以富，亦祗以異 'truly it does not lead to riches; it serves only to mark one out as strange' in Book 12 (12.10) is a displaced slip that belongs at the head of this chapter (程子以為第十二篇錯簡誠不以富亦祗以異當在此章之首); looking closely at the run of the sentences, Hu judges that it seems to belong just before this line (今詳文勢似當在此句之上) — the sense being that what people praise lies not in wealth but in being out of the common (言人之所稱不在於富而在於異也). Zhu Xi: this view is near right (愚謂此説近是), and the chapter should open with the words 孔子曰, probably lost (而章首當有孔子曰字葢闕文耳); on the whole the latter ten books of this work have many gaps and errors (大抵此書後十篇多闕誤). (At 12.10 Master Cheng is quoted as placing the couplet after 齊景公有馬千駟.) The text here is printed as it stands, with nothing moved. Wang Su in He Yan: this is what is meant by being praised for virtue (此所謂以德爲稱者也). Variant: He Yan's text reads 其斯謂與, without 之.

sentences.t:
陳亢問於伯魚曰：「
子亦有異聞乎？」
sentences.l:
Chen Kang asked of Bo Yu, saying:
“Have you, sir, had something different to hear?”
sentences.i: Chen Kang asked Bo Yu: “Has your father ever taught you something apart, sir — something the rest of us have not heard?”
sentences.n: 陳亢 Chen Kang is Ziqin 子禽 (1.10); Zhu Xi reads 亢 as gāng (亢音剛); we keep the usual kàng. 伯魚 Bo Yu is Kong Li 鯉, the Master's son (11.7). 子 'you, sir'; 亦 'indeed, after all'; 異聞 'something different heard', teaching not given to the others. Zhu Xi: Kang, peering at the sage with a private notion, suspected he must secretly favour his son (亢以私意窺聖人疑必隂厚其子). Ma Rong in He Yan: he supposed that Bo Yu, being Confucius's son, must have heard something different (以為伯魚孔子之子所聞當有異也).

sentences.t:
對曰：「
未也。
嘗獨立，鯉趨而過庭。
曰：『學《詩》乎？』
對曰：『未也。』『
不學《詩》，無以言。』
鯉退而學《詩》。」
sentences.l:
He answered, saying:
“Not yet.
Once he stood alone, and Li hurried across the courtyard.
He said: ‘Have you learned the Odes?’
I answered: ‘Not yet.’
(He said:) ‘Not learning the Odes, you have nothing to speak by.’
Li withdrew and learned the Odes.”
sentences.i: Bo Yu replied: “No. Once, when he was standing by himself, I was hurrying across the courtyard and he asked me, ‘Have you studied the Odes?’ ‘Not yet,’ I said. ‘If you have not studied the Odes, you will have nothing to draw on when you speak.’ So I went away and studied the Odes.”
sentences.n: 對曰 'answered'. 未也 'not yet', that is, no. 嘗 cháng 'once'. 獨立 'stood alone': Kong Anguo in He Yan: 'stood alone' refers to Confucius (獨立謂孔子也). 鯉 Li: Bo Yu names himself by his personal name, as one does in speaking modestly. 趨 qū 'to hurry with quick small steps', the mark of respect in passing a superior (as 9.9); 過庭 'crossed the courtyard'. 學《詩》乎 'have you learned the Odes?'. The next words have no 曰 in Zhu Xi's text, but they are the Master's: 無以言 'have nothing by which to speak' (無以 'nothing by which'). Zhu Xi: (with the Odes) one sees through the principles of affairs, and heart and spirit are calm and even, so one can speak (事理通達而心氣和平故能言); cf. 13.5, where the Odes are what an envoy is meant to answer with. Bo Yu's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next two units are left unquoted. Variant: He Yan's text reads 未也曰不學詩無以言也, marking the Master's reply with 曰 and closing with 也.

sentences.t:
他日，又獨立，鯉趨而過庭。
曰：「學禮乎？」
對曰：「未也。」「
不學禮，無以立。」
鯉退而學禮。
sentences.l:
Another day he again stood alone, and Li hurried across the courtyard.
He said: “Have you learned the rites?”
I answered: “Not yet.”
(He said:) “Not learning the rites, you have nothing to stand by.”
Li withdrew and learned the rites.
sentences.i: Another day, when he was again standing by himself and I was hurrying across the courtyard, he asked, “Have you studied the rites?” “Not yet,” I said. “If you have not studied the rites, you will have nothing to stand on.” So I went away and studied the rites.
sentences.n: Still Bo Yu, unquoted, so the exchange inside takes first-level marks. 他日 'another day'. The second scene repeats the first word for word, with 禮 'the rites' for 《詩》 and 立 'to stand' for 言. 立 'to stand, to take one's place' (as 2.4 三十而立 and 8.8 立於禮 'stands firm by the rites'). Zhu Xi: (with the rites) the grades and measures are detailed and clear, and one's virtuous nature firm and settled, so one can stand (品節詳明而徳性堅定故能立). Variant: He Yan's text reads 無以立也.

sentences.t: 聞斯二者。
sentences.l: These two things I have heard.
sentences.i: Those two things are what I have heard from him.
sentences.n: Still Bo Yu, unquoted. 斯 'these'; 二者 'the two things'. Zhu Xi: when he stood alone, what was heard went no further than this, so it can be known there was nothing different heard (當獨立之時所聞不過如此其無異聞可知). Variant: He Yan's text reads 聞斯二矣 'these two I have heard, and that is it'.

sentences.t:
陳亢退而喜，曰：「
問一得三：
聞《詩》，聞禮，
又聞君子之逺其子也。」

morph.gloss: Chen, a state south-west of Lu
in 陳亢 Chen Kang, a personal name (16.13)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
(makes 'the gentleman keeps his son at a distance' one phrase)

sentences.l:
Chen Kang withdrew, and was glad, and said:
“Asking one, I have gained three:
I heard about the Odes, I heard about the rites,
and I also heard of the gentleman's keeping his son at a distance.”
sentences.i: Chen Kang went away pleased. “One question put, and three things to take away,” he said. “I learned about the Odes, I learned about the rites, and I learned that a gentleman holds his own son no closer than his other pupils.”
sentences.n: 問一得三 'asked one, got three'. 君子之逺其子 'the gentleman's keeping his son far off': 之 makes the clause one phrase, the object of 聞. 逺 is the edition's form of 遠; as a verb, 'to keep at a distance', Zhu Xi reads it yuàn (逺去聲); modern practice reads yuǎn. 子 'son'. Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: Confucius taught his son no differently from his disciples, and so Chen Kang took it that he kept his son at a distance (孔子之教其子無異於門人故陳亢以為逺其子). Variant: He Yan's text reads 陳亢退喜, without 而.

sentences.t:
邦君之妻，
君稱之曰夫人；
夫人自稱曰小童；
邦人稱之曰君夫人，
稱諸異邦曰寡小君；
異邦人稱之亦曰君夫人。
sentences.i: The wife of a ruler is called “the Lady” by her husband, and calls herself “little child”. The people of her own state call her “our lord's Lady”; when they speak of her to other states they call her “our humble Little Lord”; and people from other states also call her “the lord's Lady”.
sentences.n: Neither 子曰 nor 孔子曰: the chapter is a bare list of titles. 邦君之妻 'the wife of a state's ruler' (邦君 as 3.22; 妻 qī 'wife'). Most lines have the shape X稱之曰Y 'X calls her Y'. 夫人 fū rén 'the Lady'; 小童 xiǎo tóng 'little child', a modest self-name. 稱諸異邦 'speaking of her to other states': 諸 is 之於 'her to'. 寡 'scant': Zhu Xi: 寡 is 'scant in virtue', a modest word (寡寡徳謙辭); 小君 xiǎo jūn 'Little Lord'. Zhu Xi quotes Wu (吳氏): wherever the book records something of this kind, one cannot tell what it is meant to say; perhaps it was so of old, perhaps the Master once said it — it cannot be checked (或古有之或夫子嘗言之不可考也). Kong Anguo in He Yan: 小君 is a name for the lord's lady; to other states one speaks modestly, hence 寡小君; at that time the wives and concubines of the lords were not kept in their places, nor their titles made exact, and so Confucius set out the rites for it (當此時諸侯嫡妾不正稱號不審故孔子正言其禮也). So ends the book. Variant: He Yan's text ends 亦曰君夫人也.
